en: Translated by Imperial Decree by Song Guṇabhadra;
annotated together by Imperial Decree by the Subject Monk Zongle, Abbot of the Chan Temple Shanshi in the Celestial Realm of Great Ming,
and the Subject Monk Ruxi, Abbot of the Lecture Temple Yanfu.
Mahāmati spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
“As the World-Honored One has said:
‘By means of various conceptualizations, one conceptualizes various natures; yet those intrinsic natures do not exist, for they are merely the nature of conceptualization.’”
"World-Honored One!

If it is only the imagined nature that lacks intrinsic nature, and if intrinsic nature exists only in mutual dependence, does this not result in the fault that the World-Honored One has thus taught that both affliction and purity lack intrinsic nature?"
"Because all phenomena are of the nature of false conceptualization and lack intrinsic reality.

This passage, beginning with "As the World-Honored One has said," represents Mahāmati’s reception of the Tathāgata’s intended meaning regarding various forms of conceptualization, serving as the opening for his inquiry.
The phrase "this and that" refers precisely to those various false conceptualizations (*vikalpa*).

Since all phenomena (*dharma*) fundamentally lack an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and exist merely as false imputations, Mahāmati still harbors a doubt: he wonders if, since these are merely the nature of false conceptualization and not phenomena possessing an intrinsic nature, this "nature" and its "lack of nature" are mutually dependent; is it not then the case, as the World-Honored One has taught, that all phenomena—whether defiled or pure—are devoid of real intrinsic nature?
Mahāmati thought that because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it would be difficult for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) to possess an intrinsic nature.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said."
"Mahāmati! It is not as the deluded worldlings falsely imagine the self-nature of things to be real; this imagined self-nature does not possess the characteristics of a true self-nature.

However, in his reply, [the Buddha] first accords with that statement, asserting that all phenomena lack self-nature, and that while they are merely imagined, to claim they possess a self-nature is erroneous.
The phrase "not like foolish people and the like" means that it is not the same as those ordinary worldlings who take the false conceptualization of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) to be real.
Furthermore, regarding the passage "this false conceptualized nature," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"This is merely a false attachment; no such nature or characteristic exists."

“Mahāmati! Just as there is the self-nature of noble wisdom, which is known by noble knowledge, seen by noble vision, and perceived by the noble eye of wisdom—in this same way, one knows that self-nature.”
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:

“If it is as the Noble Ones do—with noble knowledge, noble vision, and the noble eye of wisdom—knowing the self-nature of things as it is, rather than with the divine eye, the fleshly eye, or the deluded imaginings of fools;”
"World-Honored One!
How is it that foolish commoners are separated from this false conceptualization, yet fail to realize the reality of the noble nature?
World-Honored One!"
That is neither inverted nor non-inverted. Why is this so?
Because they do not awaken to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the reality of the noble ones, and because they do not perceive that which is free from the marks of existence and non-existence.
The previous statement that "intrinsic nature is non-nature" serves to eliminate conceptual attachment;
this present statement that "there is an intrinsic nature of nature" serves to reveal the principle.

However, this suchness of the rational nature cannot be known or seen except by the Buddha's wisdom and the Buddha's eye; therefore, it is said to be "the knowledge of the sages" and "the vision of the sages," and so forth.
Once the Buddha had revealed his own realized realm to him, Mahāmati immediately attained insight into this principle and further requested:
"If it is indeed as the Noble One knows and sees—being a wisdom and vision that is not ordinary—then it is said to be neither the divine eye nor the fleshly eye, and so forth."
Because he was again filled with doubt, he raised this objection:
"If ordinary people cannot awaken to the reality of the noble self-nature, how can they transcend false conceptualization and clearly understand this principle?"
Because the perceptions of the supreme sages and ordinary beings differ, it is said: "That is neither inverted nor non-inverted.
He further provides a self-exegesis, stating that for those who do not realize the nature of the sages' affairs, one says that ordinary beings are not non-inverted.
Not seeing anything apart from the marks of existence and non-existence means that the Sage is not deluded.
This is because everything seen by the Sage’s eye is without exception true, for he does not see a single dharma that can be abandoned.
“World-Honored One!
The Noble Ones do not perceive things in this way, for they do not take the realm of imagined characteristics as their own objective realm.
World-Honored One!”

That too is the characteristic of the self-nature of things; thus does the imagined nature appear. It is not taught because of the absence of causes, for that would entail falling into the view of [inherent] characteristics. Since the objects of experience are different from those [imagined natures], such an infinite regress would follow.
World-Honored One!
It is because they do not perceive the nature, self-nature, or characteristics [of things].
World-Honored One!

"Nor is it the nature of false imagination, because it possesses the characteristics of causal nature. How then can one falsely imagine or not falsely imagine, and know false imagination as it truly is?
As for "the noble ones do not [perceive] in such a manner," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"The noble ones do not attain things as they are discriminated by ordinary people, because [those things] are not the characteristics of the sphere of their own direct experience."

Regarding "that too is the nature of self-nature": this means that even the noble ones possess a true nature and characteristic; since the noble ones possess this nature, foolish commoners certainly possess it as well. Therefore, it is said: "The self-nature of false discrimination manifests in this way."

However, the true nature and characteristics of the Tathāgata are free from both causal conditions and the state of causelessness; yet the imagined nature of the deluded common person falls into the view of substantial characteristics.

Since the sphere of practice of the Noble Ones differs from that of ordinary fools, they do not fall into the error of an infinite regress regarding nature and characteristics, for they are able to realize the self-nature of the nature and its characteristics.

Nor is it the case that the self-nature and so forth are mere false conceptualization (*vikalpa*); since it is said that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena do not arise from discrimination, how can one say they exist through discrimination?
Therefore, the difficulty is summarized as follows:
How can those ordinary worldlings attain [the realization] that false conceptualization is not false conceptualization, such that they know reality as it is—that conceptualization is unreal?
“World-Honored One!
Conceptual construction is distinct from the characteristics of intrinsic nature.
World-Honored One!”
The dissimilar cause is the characteristic of the imagined nature; how is it that these are not individually imagined, yet foolish people do not know them as they truly are?
Nevertheless, for the sake of causing sentient beings to abandon imagination, I teach that the characteristics of the imagined are not real as they are imagined.
World-Honored One!

For what reason do you prohibit sentient beings from clinging to the views of existence and non-existence regarding the intrinsic nature of things, and yet, while prohibiting clinging to the sphere of activity of noble wisdom as falling into the view of existence, you speak of the emptiness of dharmas as being without intrinsic nature, and then speak of the intrinsic nature of the reality of noble wisdom?

The statement regarding "the difference of false conceptualization" and so forth means that ordinary people differentiate based on their own discrimination, perceiving differences in the nature and characteristics of all phenomena.

The statement regarding "dissimilar causes" means that because the perceived causes are dissimilar, how could all phenomena be permanent? They merely claim for themselves whether they are different or not different.
"Each and every" refers to all phenomena (*dharmas*); it is merely that foolish worldlings are unable to know and perceive them as they truly are.
However, when the Tathāgata speaks thus of all phenomena, it is to cause sentient beings to abandon deluded conceptualization and to realize that all phenomena are not substantially existent.

World-Honored One, for what reason do you first speak of how one should cause sentient beings to cease clinging to the views of existence and non-existence, and yet later describe taking up attachment to the realm of noble wisdom, thereby falling into the view of existence? Furthermore, for what reason do you not teach the dharma of empty quiescence, but instead speak of the intrinsic nature and phenomena of noble wisdom?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"It is not that I teach emptiness as the absence of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*); nor do I fall into the view of existence by speaking of the reality of the self-nature of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*). Rather, it is for the sake of causing sentient beings to abandon phrases that provoke fear."

Since beginningless time, sentient beings have been attached to the characteristics of the self-nature of things and to the views that cling to the self-nature of the objects of noble wisdom; for their sake, I teach the Dharma of emptiness, Mahāmati.
I do not speak of the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of things (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), Mahāmati.

Rather, I abide in the realization of the emptiness of dharmas as they truly are; I am free from the perceptions of the signs of delusion, free from the views of existence and non-existence regarding what is manifested by one's own mind, and have attained the three liberations. Sealed by the seal of reality, I abide in the observation of self-realized wisdom regarding the intrinsic nature of things, free from the views and signs of entities characterized by existence and non-existence.
In the response, he first dispels that objection.

Regarding the phrase "free from fear," it means that because sentient beings experience fear upon hearing of emptiness and attachment upon hearing of existence, he teaches the reality of the self-nature of noble wisdom to guide them.

However, the reality of noble wisdom is certainly neither existent nor non-existent; yet for those who are attached to existence, the Dharma of emptiness is taught to remedy that. Thus we know that both the teaching of emptiness and the teaching of existence are for the sake of sentient beings, and never for the purpose of asserting the existence of real dharmas. Therefore it is said: "I do not speak of the characteristics of self-nature. This indicates the dharma of personal realization by saying: "But I have attained the dharma of emptiness as it truly is," which is precisely the primordially abiding, ultimate, wondrous emptiness.

Not falling into the delusions of false inversions, one always abides in the Middle Way; thus, by departing from all views concerning the existence or non-existence of what is manifested by one's own mind, one immediately attains awakening to the three gates of liberation, acquires the seal of reality (*yathābhūta-mudrā*), perceives the self-nature of phenomena, realizes the realm of the sages, and becomes free from all attachments to existence and non-existence.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should not establish the thesis that 'all dharmas are unarisen. Why is this? "

This means that because you maintain the thesis that all natures are non-natures, and because of the characteristics of their causes and arising, your thesis that all phenomena are unarisen is undermined.
That thesis—that all phenomena are unarisen—is undermined because a thesis arises only in dependence upon something else.

Furthermore, regarding that school’s thesis of non-arising: because it enters into all phenomena and because the non-arising of unchanging characteristics is established, the thesis of the non-arising of all phenomena put forward by them is thereby undermined.
Mahāmati! The thesis that neither existence nor non-existence arises enters into all natures, for the characteristics of existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended. Mahāmati!

If one were to establish a thesis by asserting that all natures are unarisen so as to prevent that [opposing] thesis from arising, then that thesis would be undermined; because the characteristics of existence and non-existence are unarisen, one should not establish a thesis.

Because the five-membered syllogism involves many fallacies, because its successive members possess distinct characteristics, and because it functions as a means of proof, one should not establish the thesis-position (pakṣa) that "all phenomena are unarisen."
"Since all phenomena are empty in this way, and all phenomena lack intrinsic nature in this way, one should not establish a thesis.
The preceding statement that both discursive thought and noble wisdom are empty means that both the true and the false are discarded; this is the meaning of non-arising.
Fearing that a Bodhisattva might establish this as a thesis and thereby become confused with externalist views, he spoke these words to refute it.

To say that "all phenomena are unarisen" is already to transcend both speech and conceptualization; since even such a statement is already not [ultimately] true, how much more so the arbitrary establishment of a thesis?

Just as those non-Buddhists establish the thesis of "non-arising" (anutpāda) and thereby produce further conceptual proliferation, it is said that "one should not establish such a thesis. Why is this?

The following passage interrogates and explains its meaning: regarding the thesis that "all natures are non-natures," the intent is that a thesis must necessarily have a subject. If one takes "all natures" as the thesis, yet the natures themselves are non-natures, where then does the meaning of the thesis reside?

Generally speaking, the term "non-arising" must be established in dependence upon "arising. Since there is thus a mutual dependence and opposition, non-arising would become arising; this would inherently subvert the meaning of non-arising. This is the first reason why such a thesis should not be established.

Furthermore, that school’s position on non-arising must necessarily be included within all phenomena. To say that the meaning of non-arising pervades all phenomena in the world, and that it is called "non-arising" because its unchanging nature does not arise, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"The characteristic of non-arising is itself non-arising; therefore, it is said that all phenomena are fundamentally non-arising—how could they wait for [the act of] establishment!"
Therefore, it is said that their doctrine is undermined; this is the second reason why they should not establish a thesis.

Regarding the statement that "existence and non-existence do not arise," previously [the opponent] held that non-existence does not arise; now, however, they shift their calculation to claim that both existence and non-existence do not arise.

Regarding the statement "entering all natures," nature is precisely the Dharma. This means that neither existence nor non-existence arises, and it pervades all phenomena; all are devoid of the characteristics of existence and non-existence. Even if one were to further calculate and conceptualize the natures and characteristics of existence and non-existence, none can be apprehended. This is also the meaning of non-arising, and thus the third point regarding the non-establishment of a thesis.
Regarding "the five-membered syllogism having many fallacies": the meaning of the five-membered syllogism is seen in the preceding notes.
"Many fallacies" refers to the fallacies of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

First, there are nine fallacies of the thesis, namely: contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa-viruddha*), contradiction with authoritative scripture (*āgama-viruddha*), contradiction with worldly consensus (*loka-viruddha*), contradiction with inference (*anumāna-viruddha*), contradiction with one's own words (*svavacana-viruddha*), that which is already established by agreement (*siddhasādhana*), the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) being unestablished, the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) being unestablished, and both the qualifier and the qualificand being unestablished.

Next, there are fourteen fallacies based on that [definition]. Regarding the first characteristic, "the property being present in the entirety of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*), there are four types of "unestablished" (*asiddha*): namely, unestablished for one party (*anyatarāsiddha*), unestablished regarding the locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), unestablished for both parties (*ubhayāsiddha*), and unestablished due to doubt (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*).

The latter two types of fallacies comprise ten faults in total, of which six are "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*): namely, the inconclusive based on similarity and difference in their entirety, the inconclusive based on difference and similarity in their entirety, the inconclusive based on partial occurrence in both categories, the common inconclusive, the uncommon inconclusive, and the inconclusive due to contradictory determination. There are four types of "contradictory" (*viruddha*) fallacies:

namely, contradiction regarding the self-characteristic of the property (*dharma-svalakṣaṇa-viruddha*), contradiction regarding the specific distinction of the property (*dharma-viśeṣa-viruddha*), contradiction regarding the self-characteristic of the subject (*dharmin-svalakṣaṇa-viruddha*), and contradiction regarding the specific distinction of the subject (*dharmin-viśeṣa-viruddha*).
The similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) has five fallacies, and the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) also has five fallacies.

Regarding the similar instance, they are: the unestablishedness of the probandum (*sādhyāsiddha*), the unestablishedness of the probans (*sādhanāsiddha*), the unestablishedness of both (*ubhayāsiddha*), the lack of connection (*ayojita*), and the inverted connection (*viparīta-yojita*).

In the section on "dissimilar examples" (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), it is said: "the probans is not excluded, the probandum is not excluded, both are not excluded, non-separation, and inverted separation.
These constitute thirty-three fallacies in total.

Regarding "successive differences in causes": this refers to their shifting arguments that the characteristics of causes differ, thereby falling into the errors of being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and produced (*kṛtaka*); this is the fourth point regarding why their thesis should not be established.

Furthermore, it is said that all dharmas are unarisen, it is said they are empty, and it is said they lack intrinsic nature. If these three were each established as a thesis, there would be many theses; thus, it is improper to establish a thesis in five ways.

“Mahāmati! However, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas teach that all dharmas are like illusions and dreams, it is because they manifest both appearing and non-appearing characteristics, and because they perceive the faults of [dualistic] views and cognitions. Therefore, they should explain that the nature of all dharmas is like illusions and dreams, so as not to cause others to become terrified and abandon the Mahāyāna.”

Having already rejected the fallacy of establishing a formal thesis (pakṣa), he now demonstrates its correctness; thus, he says to Mahāmati: "One should explain that all phenomena possess the characteristics of appearing and not appearing like illusions and dreams."
"Manifest" and "non-manifest" refer to the fact that [phenomena] do not truly exist.
Furthermore, it is for the sake of causing sentient beings to abandon the faults of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.

It further states, "I shall explain," which excludes those who are foolish; for the foolish fall into the views of existence and non-existence, and if one does not teach that [phenomena] are like illusions or dreams, they cannot abandon those two views.

Furthermore, fearing that those of inferior capacity might hear this teaching of "neither being nor non-being" and thereby give rise to fear, refusing to accept the Mahāyāna, he cautioned: "Do not cause them to be terrified and thus abandon the Mahāyāna. The intent is for the Bodhisattva to preach the Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Without intrinsic nature and without expression, without objective reality and without continuity—
these are the false imaginings of the foolish, like the evil perceptions of a corpse.”
All phenomena are unarisen; this is not the tenet of those non-Buddhists.
Ultimately there is nothing that arises; they are accomplished through the nature of conditions.
All phenomena are unarisen; the wise do not form conceptualizations of them.
"Because that school [asserts] arising, the Awakened One has completely eliminated it.
This verse above states that all phenomena are unarisen; since all phenomena fundamentally lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how could there be verbal expression?
Where there is no discourse, there is no objective reality; where there is no objective reality, there is no characteristic of continuity; thus, both the root and the branches are non-arising.
It is only those deluded fools who falsely give rise to discrimination and establish the thesis of "non-arising"; their evil perceptions are like a corpse devoid of consciousness.
Thus, when the Buddha says that all phenomena are unarisen, how could this be the same as the doctrine of "non-arising" established by those non-Buddhists?

[The Buddha’s teaching] means that ultimately there is nothing produced; it speaks of the nature being fundamentally unarisen, yet arising from causes and conditions. Since even causes and conditions cannot be apprehended, how could any phenomena have an arising?
However, since the wise do not even form the notion of non-arising, how could they form the notion of arising?
When that school speaks of "non-arising," it is because there is non-arising by virtue of arising; thus, it remains subject to relative dependence.
The Awakened One has no such views; therefore, it is said that they are "all eliminated.
"Just as one with cataracts sees, Falsely perceiving the appearance of falling hair, So too is the nature of clinging: The false conceptualization of the deluded."
In the three realms of existence, there is no intrinsic nature to things;
yet, by designating an intrinsic nature to things, one gives rise to delusive conceptualization through reflection.
When signs and things are used to establish verbal teachings, the mind becomes distracted, trembling and shaking violently.
"The Buddha-sons are able to transcend and remain far removed from all delusive thoughts.

This is like the case of those with cataracts in their eyes; it clarifies the distinction between the false and the correct. "Cataracts in the eyes" and "hanging hairs" are both explained in the preceding notes as metaphors for that which does not exist yet appears to do so.

The three realms of existence are the triple world; that is to say, the three realms of existence are fundamentally non-existent, appearing only through deluded imagination. Therefore it is said: "The three realms of existence are merely conventional designations; they have no intrinsic nature of their own."

"Provisional designation" (prajñapti) means establishment; it arises from conceptual construction (vikalpa), and for this reason the Tathāgata establishes verbal teachings to transform beings—namely, "using only provisional names to guide sentient beings."

Sentient beings fail to comprehend this and, contrary to the verbal teachings, give rise to discrimination, thereby agitating and disturbing their consciousness; hence it is said, "the mind is disordered and violently shaken.
Only the Bodhisattvas can distance themselves from these faults and transcend the three realms of existence.
"To perceive water where there is no water is a sensation born of craving;
the deluded person is thus confused, but for the noble one it is not so.
The noble one perceives purity, arising from the three liberations and samādhi."
Far removed from arising and ceasing, one wanders in non-existence.
Practicing in non-existence, there is neither nature nor non-nature;
with nature and non-nature being equal, from this the fruits of the noble ones arise.

"Regarding 'perceiving what is not water as water': this refers to falsely conceiving what is not water to be water due to the influence of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). It is like a thirsty deer rushing toward a mirage; this metaphor illustrates how the foolish person perceives that which does not exist as existing."
The Sage is not so; for the Sage perceives the characteristics of the three realms through correct wisdom as being devoid of afflictions and birth-and-death, and thus they are called pure.

The three liberations are wisdom, and samādhi is concentration. Once concentration and wisdom have arisen, one departs from birth and extinction and wanders within non-existence; non-existence is precisely ultimate emptiness.

Regarding the statement "practicing non-existence," it means that when a bodhisattva is able to practice in this manner, they also accord with the principle of being neither existent nor non-existent; therefore, it is said: "neither having nature nor lacking nature."
In this way, existence and non-existence are equal, and the fruit of Buddhahood is accomplished.
"What is meant by 'nature' and 'non-nature'?
What constitutes equality?"
"It means that when that mind does not know, it is extremely agitated both internally and externally;
if one can destroy that [agitation], the mind will then perceive with equanimity.
The Buddha himself provides this self-exegesis, meaning that existence and non-existence are equal, and ordinary beings and sages are of one suchness, differing only due to delusion and awakening.
In delusion, one does not know that there are no phenomena outside the mind, and is thus drifted and tossed about by the winds of objective conditions;
through understanding, one is able to destroy those views and thereby restore the principle of the equality of the fundamental mind.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has taught, when wisdom does not apprehend an object through its causal conditions, this is established as the measure of designation."

That which is grasped by conceptual designation (*prajñapti*) is without intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*), and the grasping itself is also without intrinsic nature. Because there is no grasping, cognition does not arise; it is merely a name established by designation.
Since it was previously explained that wisdom is characterized by being free from objective referents (*ālambana*), he again requests [instruction] on the basis that wisdom cannot be apprehended.

As the World-Honored One said regarding "objects of apprehension," the sensory objects of the world are the things apprehended by the ignorant; when observed with right knowledge, they are found to be non-existent. Therefore, it is said: "One does not obtain this measure of designation or its establishment."

The "provisional establishment" refers to the objective realms constructed by the aforementioned deluded conceptualization. Since these objective realms cannot be found, both the grasper and the grasped are non-existent; therefore, it is said that cognition does not arise. All that is provisionally established is merely a false name based on deluded conceptualization.
“World-Honored One, is it because wisdom does not apprehend due to the nature of the self-characteristic and common characteristic being neither different nor non-different?
Or is it because wisdom does not apprehend due to the various natures and intrinsic characteristics of the self-characteristic and common characteristic being obscured?”
Is it because of obstructions such as mountains, crags, stone walls, earth, water, fire, or wind that wisdom cannot be attained?
Is it because of being too far away or too near that wisdom cannot be attained?
Or is it because of being old, young, blind, or lacking in the sensory faculties that wisdom cannot be attained?
World-Honored One!

If one does not perceive whether self-characteristics and common characteristics are different or non-different, and thus cognition is unattainable, then one should not speak of "cognition," but rather speak of "non-cognition," because there is an object that cannot be attained.

Furthermore, World-Honored One, if wisdom cannot apprehend because the various specific and general characteristics and intrinsic natures are obscured by their own inherent characteristics, then that [wisdom] is itself non-wisdom; it is not true wisdom.
World-Honored One!
Because there is an object (*ālambana*), knowledge arises; it is not that knowledge exists by meeting with an object that lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

If knowledge were unable to apprehend mountain crags, rocky walls, earth, water, fire, wind, things extremely distant or extremely near, or things belonging to the old, the young, the blind, or those with impaired faculties, this would likewise not be knowledge, but rather a lack of knowledge, because the object exists yet cannot be apprehended.

The Master replied: "I have already explained that wisdom cannot be attained; yet, fearing that students may not fully understand, I have restated the intent of my several questions to cause them to shatter false wisdom and reveal true wisdom. Therefore, I have repeatedly raised challenges by juxtaposing each instance of false wisdom with its opposite."

The initial statement, "Is it because one does not study the self-characteristics, common characteristics, and so forth? means that regarding all phenomena such as the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas), one has no realization that they possess self-characteristics and common characteristics, nor whether they are different or not different; therefore, it asks, "Is it because wisdom does not apprehend them?"
Furthermore, it is asked: "Is it because [the object] is obscured by the self-natures and characteristics of various phenomena—both specific and general—that it cannot become wisdom?
As for the following objections, wisdom would not be wisdom, and moreover, this does not resolve the issue.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not so.

Non-intelligence should be intelligence, not non-intelligence. I do not speak of the concealment of the objects of perception such that wisdom cannot be attained; rather, this is an establishment based on the measure of conventional designation."
Realizing that what appears to one's own mind is merely a mental construct, and knowing that there are no external entities or non-entities, one finds nothing to be grasped.
Because nothing is found, cognition does not arise toward objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), and even the wisdom that accords with the three gates of liberation is not apprehended.

"Non-delusive conceptualization" refers to the knowledge produced by the habitual tendencies of false discrimination regarding the nature and non-nature of things since beginningless time; such knowledge is "knowing that [the other] does not know.
In the response, the phrase "it is not so" serves to dispel that objection.
Regarding the phrase "non-wisdom" (*ajñāna*) and so forth: it is the wisdom that is not [ordinary] wisdom, yet even the essence of wisdom cannot be apprehended;

therefore, it is called "not non-wisdom. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, "non-wisdom" refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*); "wisdom" refers to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*); and "not non-wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-prajñā*). These three wisdoms are attained within a single moment of mind; though attained, there is no attainment—this is what is meant by "the non-apprehension of wisdom."

Regarding the statement, "I do not speak thus in a concealed manner," the Buddha said that my speaking thus is explicit and not concealed. Although there are indeed always teachings spoken in a concealed manner—as indicated by the subsequent passages—whenever it was appropriate to conceal, I concealed; whenever it was appropriate to reveal, I revealed. This [present teaching], however, is not concealed.

Below the section "Awakening to the Manifestation of One’s Own Mind," the true wisdom is correctly revealed; that is to say, one realizes that the existence or non-existence of objects is merely the measure of one's own mind.
The statement that "external nature is neither existent nor non-existent" means that all phenomena are fundamentally empty.
To know in this manner, yet to know while not knowing, is what is meant by "the object is not attained. The "object" (事) is the "境" (境, *viṣaya*).

Since the object is not attained, wisdom (*jñāna*) likewise does not arise; this is the obstruction of the knowledge of the *jñeyāvaraṇa*. Upon entering the three gates of liberation, even the essence of wisdom perishes.

"Non-delusory thought" distinguishes it from delusory cognition; that is to say, it is not like the wisdom of ordinary people who, since beginningless time, possess the delusory habitual tendencies of existence and non-existence. Such individuals do not know that all phenomena are mind-only; they perceive external objects but do not know their own nature, thereby losing their wisdom to things. Hence it is said: "This is knowing, while that is not knowing."

"Therefore, regarding external objects, their locations, characteristics, and the absence of intrinsic nature, one's false conceptualization remains uninterrupted. One establishes [a view] based on the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind, speaking of the characteristics of 'I' and 'mine,' grasping at them with attachment. Failing to realize that these are manifestations of one's own mind, one gives rise to false conceptualization regarding knowledge (*jñāna*) and the knowable (*jñeya*)."
"Because of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one fails to perceive that external natures are neither existent nor non-existent, and thus relies upon the view of annihilationism.

This follows from what was stated above; it means that such deluded cognition regarding external objects does not cease its discrimination between existence and non-existence of forms. This is a false construction established by oneself within the measure of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśya-mātra*). By calculating the two selves of person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-ātman*), one gives rise to grasping and attachment. Indeed, failing to realize that this is the measure of one's own mind, one does not sever the false conceptualization regarding the aforementioned external objects and falls into the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).

Subsequently, regarding the essence of wisdom where subject and object are not delusive, one instead gives rise to conceptualization by turning it into an obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); because of this conceptualization, one observes external phenomena as either existent or non-existent, and thus gives rise to the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) within the state where neither can be apprehended.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"When there are objects of perception, if wisdom does not examine them, this is a lack of wisdom, not true wisdom; so say those who harbor false imaginings."
When wisdom does not discern the nature of non-differentiation,
nor the obstacles, the distant, or the near, this is called false wisdom.
When the faculties of the old and the young are obscured, wisdom does not arise.
"If there were actually such an object of cognition (*jñeya*), this too would be called false wisdom.
That which has an objective realm as its object is the wisdom of ordinary beings;
that which realizes the object is nothing but mind is the wisdom of correct wisdom.
If correct wisdom were to take what is without an object as its object, it would be non-wisdom.
To claim that this non-wisdom constitutes "not being wise" is merely the conceptual fabrication of ordinary people.
This verse explains the meaning of the aforementioned non-attainment of wisdom.

Regarding the statement "wisdom does not observe the nature of non-differentiation," this verse refers to the aforementioned distinction and non-distinction between specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
"To say 'not observing' means that wisdom does not attain [its object].
The rest is all visible as a verse summarizing the above.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!"

Foolish ordinary beings are turned around by beginningless, false, evil, and perverse conceptualizations. While being thus turned around, they do not properly understand the thorough realization of one's own school (*svapratyātmagatigocara*) or the teaching of the doctrine (*deśanā*). Because they cling to the external characteristics of natures manifested by their own minds, they cling to expedient teachings and fail to correctly discern the pure characteristics of the fourfold logical alternatives (*catuskoṭi*) within their own school.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“It is truly as Your Majesty has taught.

I only pray that the World-Honored One will, for my sake, analyze and explain the *sūtra-vehicle* (the teaching) and the *principle-vehicle* (the realization). May I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas become proficient in these two vehicles, so that in future ages ordinary people, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas shall find no flaw in them.”
Regarding the statement that the "common characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) have already been explained, why are they stated again here?
Previously, they pertained to all three vehicles; here, they pertain solely to the Buddha.
Furthermore, previously it was requested by the assembly; here, the Buddha describes them himself.

Regarding the phrase "foolish ordinary beings and the like," it means that these two dharmas have never been absent from ordinary beings; however, because they are deluded and transmigrating, they do not know them at all.

"Reversal" refers to turning inward and outward due to delusion regarding one's own self; it means being attached solely to external objects such as the manifestations of one's own mind, and likewise being attached to the verbal teachings of skillful means. Consequently, one fails to clearly comprehend the pure nature that transcends the four extremes, which is the fundamental essence of one's own mind. For this reason, Mahāmati subsequently made his request.
Regarding the statement that one must not be deficient: if the principle (zong) is realized but the teaching (shuo) is not, the deficiency lies in the guidance of others;
if the teaching is realized but the principle is not, the deficiency lies in one's own practice.
If both are mutually pervasive, then they cannot be considered limited.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Excellent!"
Excellent! Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
"Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for your sake.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction."
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

“The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time possess two kinds of dharma-attainment: namely, the attainment of the teaching (*deśanā-prativedha*) and the attainment of one’s own school (*sva-siddhānta-prativedha*).

As for the attainment of the teaching, it refers to preaching various sūtras and collections of teachings according to what is appropriate for the minds of sentient beings; this is called the attainment of the teaching.”

Regarding the "thorough penetration of one's own school" (*svapratyātma-gatigocara*): it refers to the practitioner who is free from the various delusive imaginings manifested by their own mind; that is, not falling into the categories of identity, difference, both, or neither; transcending all mind, intellect, and consciousness; realizing the noble realm of self-awakening; and being free from the characteristics of views produced by causes. This is something that cannot be known by any non-Buddhists, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or those fallen into the two extremes. I declare this to be the teaching of the thorough penetration of one's own school.
"Mahāmati! These are called the characteristics of the penetration of one's own school and the penetration of teaching; you and the other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice and study them.

In the answer, it is stated that the Tathāgatas of the three periods possess these two penetrations; this reveals that there is no difference in the dharmas by which all Buddhas cultivate themselves and transform others.
First, the general teaching is explained.

Regarding the term "Sūtras of All Requisites" (*sarvopakaraṇa-sūtra*): this refers to the aforementioned nine divisions [of the scriptures], which are called "all requisites" because they encompass all dharmas; yet, as they ultimately accord with principle and accord with the capacities [of sentient beings], they are termed "Sūtras" (*sūtra*).

Next, the principle of the ultimate teaching (*zongtong*) is clarified. The Dharma of self-realization is fundamentally inexpressible; therefore, it is manifested through its characteristics by means of those who practice.

To say "transcending the various deluded thoughts manifested by one's own mind" means not falling into the four propositions, such as unity or difference; when deluded thoughts do not function, one transcends all mental consciousness and reaches the state of the noble ones' self-awakening.

Regarding the phrase "separation from the perception established by causes": "established by causes" refers to the conventional designation of being established by causes, meaning that the mental faculty (*manas*) arises in relation to mental objects (*dharmas*) to produce discriminative perception; "separation" means to be free from this perception.

However, the Dharma personally realized by the Tathāgata cannot be known by those who are heterodox, external, partial, or small-minded, nor by those attached to the two extremes of existence and emptiness; it can only be cultivated and realized by Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas. Therefore, it is admonished that "one should cultivate and study it."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"I speak of two kinds of penetration: The penetration of the principle and the penetration of verbal expression.
Verbal expression is taught to the ignorant; The principle is for those who practice."

"Childish and ignorant" refers to those at the initial stage of practice; however, once one has attained thorough understanding and explanation, it does not necessarily apply only to beginners—it is said in contrast to "penetration of the principle" (*zongtong*).
Although penetration of the principle pertains to spiritual cultivation, it specifically refers to self-realization.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One once said:”

“World-Honored One! You have said, ‘Be careful not to associate with the various arguments and diverse discourses of the world; if you associate with them, you will embrace desire and fail to embrace the Dharma.
World-Honored One!”
"For what reason do I speak thus?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"The various phrases and expressions of worldly discourse, adorned with causes, conditions, and parables, are used to entice and delude foolish ordinary people. They do not enter into the true self-realization; they do not awaken to all phenomena, but through false imagination and inversion, fall into the two extremes."

Ordinary fools, deluded by ignorance, bring about their own ruin; they continue through the various realms of existence and fail to attain liberation. Unable to realize that all things are merely the manifestations of their own minds, they do not depart from external natures and intrinsic identities, but instead cling to them through false conceptualization. Consequently, despite the various discourses and eloquent explanations of worldly treatises, they remain unable to escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, remaining deceived, deluded, and confused.

Now, regarding discourse, there are both worldly discourse (*lokavāda*) and supramundane discourse (*lokottaravāda*); thus, the Way has both the correct and the deviant. Although these two cannot coexist, they have never ceased to proceed side by side in the world. Therefore, the Tathāgata cautioned that one must be careful not to draw near to worldly discourse, which is why Mahāmati posed his question.
As for what is called "worldly discourse" (loka-vāda), it refers to the non-Buddhist Lokāyata school; this is translated as "Left-hand World" or "Evil Discourse.
This doctrine merely adorns its rhetoric to deceive the ignorant and foolish; those who associate with it only acquire worldly wealth and desires, and do not obtain the benefit of the Dharma.

In the reply, one first refutes their error because their discourse does not elucidate correct principle; it cannot enter the domain of genuine self-realization, ultimately resulting in nothing but the two extremes.

"Ordinary fools, deluded and ignorant, below"—this clarifies that their practice of receiving [teachings] is erroneous, for by destroying their own right view, they cause the continuity of birth and death across the various realms of existence.
The causes for liberation and the characteristics of the various faults will be evident in the subsequent text.
“Mahāmati! Śakra Devendra has extensively mastered various treatises and composed his own work on phonology.
A disciple of that worldly philosopher went to the palace of Śakra, assuming the form of a nāga, and established a philosophical thesis, vowing to destroy Śakra’s thousand-spoked wheel:”
"If I am defeated, I shall cut off my head one by one to atone for my humiliation.
Having made this vow, he then used the Dharma of Śakra to subdue Śakra.
Having thus explained the points of defeat, he destroyed his chariot and returned to the human realm.

"In this way, Mahāmati, worldly discourse is adorned with causes and analogies; even animals can, by means of various phrases and expressions, delude those gods and asuras who are attached to views of arising and ceasing—how much more so, then, can humans?"
"Therefore, Mahāmati!
One should distance oneself from worldly discourse, for it brings about the causes for the arising of suffering; be careful not to cultivate or frequent it.
This section below cites examples to demonstrate the faults [of such discourse].
Śakra-devānām-indra is an alternative name for Śakra.
"Bearing the form of a dragon" means transforming into a dragon body.
"Essential" (yào) means to restrict or limit.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"Make this essential declaration: 'Kauśika!'"
"I shall debate with you; if you do not prevail over me, I shall shatter your thousand-spoked wheel.
If I do not prevail, I shall sever each of my own heads as an apology for my defeat."
"To refute by means of the Dharma of Śakra" means to use the treatises composed by Śakra as a challenge.
"Falling into defeat" means not being victorious; that is, Śakra is not victorious.
"Even down to animals" refers to those who have transformed into such forms as dragon bodies.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that one "should distance oneself from worldly treatises," it means that since these treatises can cause such harm, how could one not be cautious?
“Mahāmati! Those who propound worldly treatises speak only of the body, cognition, and their objects. Mahāmati!”

There will be hundreds of thousands of those proponents of worldly doctrines; however, in a later time, during the final fifty years, they shall destroy the communal recitation (saṃgīti), because the causes and views of evil discernment will flourish, and evil disciples will accept them.
Thus it is, Mahāmati!

Worldly treatises destroy the true compilation [of the Dharma]; they are adorned with various phrases and flavors, using causes and analogies to discourse on the matters of non-Buddhists. They are attached to their own causal conditions and possess no independent realization.

Mahāmati! Those heterodox teachers have no doctrine of their own; they extensively expound hundreds of thousands of gateways of worldly discourse, yet they possess no self-attained realization, nor do they recognize that their own teachings are merely the deluded discourse of the world.
Below, following the discussion on worldly doctrines (*lokāyata*), this treatise is presented again to establish its own position.

Regarding "the body, sensation, and the sphere of objects": this refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as the objects of the body’s perception and conceptualization. Although those worldly doctrines number in the hundreds of thousands, their ultimate tenets do not transcend emotional consciousness; how could they know of the Ultimate Way?

Regarding the statement that "in the final fifty years, the compilers of the Council will be destroyed," according to the *Vajrapuṇyadāna-śāstra*, the human lifespan of one hundred years is divided into two parts: during the first fifty years, the power of the teachings is strengthened; during the subsequent fifty years, the power of the teachings gradually diminishes. This refers to the time when the True Dharma (*saddharma*) is about to perish.

Or perhaps it will be during the final five hundred years—though the character "ten" (十) may be an error—that they will destroy the Tathāgata’s correctly compiled True Teaching. Because their inverted, evil cognitions, causes of suffering, and false views will flourish, those of their wicked faction will adopt and practice these doctrines, thereby bringing about their own downfall and drowning.
The following section concludes with a reprimand.

Regarding the phrase "clinging to one's own causes and conditions": it refers to those who, having identified the body and sensations as described above, are nonetheless unable to achieve self-comprehension through principle; hence it is said that they "lack self-comprehension."

Because they cannot communicate with themselves, even though they extensively expound upon hundreds of thousands of doctrinal gates, these do not transcend the delusive worldly dharmas; that they remain unaware of this is truly lamentable.
At that time, Mahāmati said to the Buddha:

"World-Honored One, if the various phrases, expressions, causes, and analogies used by non-Buddhists in their worldly treatises lack any self-attained realization and are merely attachments to their own affairs, then does the World-Honored One also speak of worldly treatises? For the sake of the various assemblies of gods, humans, and asuras gathered from different regions, You extensively expound immeasurable varieties of phrases and expressions; is this not also a worldly treatise lacking self-attained realization?"
"Does this also fall within the category of the wisdom and discourse of all non-Buddhist paths?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"I do not speak of worldly discourse, nor is there coming or going; I speak only of neither coming nor going."

Mahāmati! That which comes is the gathering and arising; that which goes is the dispersal and destruction. That which neither comes nor goes is neither born nor extinguished. The meaning I have taught does not fall within the categories of worldly treatises or deluded conceptualization.

Why is this so? It is because one does not cling to external existence or non-existence as the locus of what is manifested by one's own mind; thus, one cannot be turned by the false imaginings of the two extremes. When one realizes that objective marks lack inherent nature and are merely manifestations of one's own mind, then the false imaginings manifested by one's own mind will no longer arise.
"When false conceptualization does not arise, one enters the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; this is called liberation.
This reveals the true teaching.
At the outset, Mahāmati poses a counter-question, asserting that what the Tathāgata has taught is also identical to worldly discourse; this constitutes two challenges, as detailed in the text.

For instance, when he extensively expounds upon all dharmas for the sake of the devas and humans of other realms, this is speech that accords with the intentions of others—how could it not also be his own established doctrine?
Furthermore, how does this differ from the discursive speech of the worldly wisdom of non-Buddhists?
In the response, the initial objection is first set aside by stating: "I do not teach worldly discourse.
For while worldly discourse speaks of going and coming, the Buddha teaches only neither-going-nor-coming.
Regarding the statement that "coming" refers to arising through the gathering of conditions: this means that when [conditions] come together, they harmonize and give rise to existence.
Regarding the statement that "going" refers to disintegration: this means that when [conditions] depart, they scatter and [existence] ceases.
The Buddha spoke these distinct words: that which neither goes nor comes is precisely that which is neither born nor extinguished; this is what I have mastered.

In response to the subsequent objection, he stated, "It does not fall into the categories of the delusive imaginings of worldly discourse. This means that the dualistic discrimination between existence and non-existence held by non-Buddhists constitutes their delusive imaginings.
He further provides a self-verification and explanation, stating that by not clinging to the two extremes, one cannot be turned by the deluded thoughts of existence or non-existence.

This is because the realm of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); since it is without intrinsic nature, it is empty—how, then, could there be anything to turn?

Furthermore, regarding the statement "awakening to what is manifested by one's own mind" and so forth: once one has realized that all phenomena are mind-only, from where could deluded conceptualization (vikalpa) possibly arise?

Because it does not arise, one enters the three gates of liberation: "emptiness" (śūnyatā) refers to the emptiness of intrinsic nature; "signlessness" (animitta) refers to the emptiness of characteristics; and "wishlessness" (apraṇihita) refers to the emptiness of both nature and characteristics, wherein the mind performs no action.
"Non-action is also called 'wishlessness,' meaning the absence of any longing or seeking.
Mahāmati, I recall that once, while staying in a certain place, a world-theorizing brāhmaṇa came to where I was; without having requested a private audience, he immediately questioned me, saying:"
"Gautama! Is everything created? I then replied:
“Brahmin! All that is performed is the first worldly doctrine. He then asked again:
"Is everything uncreated? I replied again:
"To claim that everything is uncreated is the second worldly doctrine."
He asked again: "Is everything eternal?
Or is everything impermanent?"
"Are all beings born? Or are all beings unborn?
At that time, I replied:
"This is the doctrine of the six heretical teachers. Mahāmati!
They then asked me further:
"Are all things one? Are all things different?
Or are all things both?"
"Are all things not simultaneous?
Or do all things arise and manifest due to various causes?
To this, I replied:
"This is the eleventh worldly discourse. Mahāmati!
He then asked again:
"Are all things indeterminate?
Are all things determinate?
Does a self exist?"
Is there no self?
Does this world exist?
Or does this world not exist?
Is there a future world?
Is there no future world? Is there liberation?
Is there no liberation?
Are all things momentary?
Or are all things non-momentary?
Is it space? Is it analytical cessation?
Or is it nirvana?
"Gautama! Is there such a thing as doing what is wrong, or not doing what is wrong?
Is there an intermediate state (antarābhava)?"
"Is there no intermediate state (antarābhava)? Mahāmati! I then replied:
"O Brahmin! Such statements as these are all worldly discourses; they are not what I teach, but are your own worldly discourses.
This passage correctly cites the treatise to extensively distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.
"Brahman" is a term from the Sanskrit language; its full form is *brahmaṇa*, which is translated here as "Pure Lineage" (*jingyi*) or also as "Pure Conduct" (*xingxing*).
They claim that their ancestors were born from the mouth of Brahmā, and thus they derive their surname from Brahmā; the term "Brahmacārin" (*fanzhi*) refers precisely to this lineage.
It exists only in the five regions of India and is not found in other countries.

Furthermore, it is said that those of foreign intent have their own distinct scriptures and inherit this profession through generations; whether they remain laypeople or become renunciants, they rely on their arts to act with arrogance.

Regarding the phrase "not requesting a leisurely interval," "leisurely interval" (kōngxián) refers to a gap or opportunity. The etiquette for posing questions requires waiting for such an opportunity, just as in ritual there is the expression "requesting an interval" (qǐngjiàn).
Yet he was arrogant and suddenly came to question me; this is why I rebuked him.
Although his questions were many, I answered them collectively by discussing the retribution of a single lifetime; this is how I rejected him.
All such statements are merely worldly discourse (*lokavāda*) and do not transcend the views of ordinary beings.
Furthermore, when it is said, "This is not what I have taught; it is your worldly discourse," it is for this reason that [the Buddha] sets them aside as external.

"I teach only that beginningless false imagination and habitual tendencies are the cause of various evils and the three realms of existence. Failing to realize that these are merely manifestations of one's own mind, one gives rise to false imaginings and clings to external natures, as do the non-Buddhists who claim that knowledge arises from the conjunction of the self, the sense organs, and their objects. I do not hold such a view."

"O Brahmin! I do not speak of causes, nor do I speak of causelessness; I speak only of the nature of the grasped and the grasper as being mere conceptual construction, which is designated as dependent origination. This is not something that you or others who have fallen into the continuity of the notion of a self can perceive."
"Mahāmati! Nirvāṇa, space, and cessation do not actually exist as three kinds; there are only three enumerations.

Thus the Buddha himself demonstrates that the true teaching does not go beyond these three paths: beginningless [ignorance] up to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) constitute the path of afflictions (*kleśamārga*); [the remaining paths are the path of karma and the path of birth].
The various kinds of evils are the paths of karma;
the three realms of existence are the path of suffering.
As for "causes," this refers to afflictions and evil karma serving as the causes for the path of suffering.

Because one fails to realize that all phenomena are manifestations of mind-only, one gives rise to false conceptualizations and grasping toward those external phenomena; this is the teaching of the true causes and conditions, which is not known by the non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, the phrase "like the doctrines of the non-Buddhists" reiterates their specific calculations in order to refute their assertions.

To say that "cognition arises from the conjunction of the three—the self, the faculties, and the objects" means that cognition arises through the harmonious combination of these three conditions: the self, the sense-faculties, and the sensory domains; "cognition" here refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The Buddha’s teaching differs from this; therefore, he said, "I do not speak of causes, nor do I speak of causelessness.

"Cause" refers to causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), while "causelessness" refers to spontaneity (*svabhāva*). It is only based upon the deluded mind, through the grasping of subject and object, that one speaks of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). This is beyond the comprehension of you and other non-Buddhists who cling to the ego-grasping that is never severed.

The terms "nirvāṇa," "space," and "cessation" appear to arise in isolation; yet, upon examining Mahāmati’s question—which asserts that the Tathāgata’s teaching is identical to that of the non-Buddhist Sāṃkhya school—the Buddha declared:
"These three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) merely have three enumerations, but they do not exist as three [distinct entities]."
The meaning of the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) is as seen in the preceding note. "Furthermore, Mahāmati!
At that time, the Brahmin of Worldly Discourse again asked me: "
"Is the existence of the three realms of existence caused by ignorance,
craving, and karma, or is it without cause? I then replied:
“Both of these are merely worldly discourse.
He asked again: “Do all natures enter into their own-characteristics and common-characteristics?”
I replied again: "This, too, is worldly discourse, O Brahmin!"
"Up to and including the mental stream, all false conceptualizations of external objects are merely worldly discourse. Furthermore,
Mahāmati, at that time the world-discourse Brahmin again asked me:
"Are there any who are not proponents of worldly discourse?
I am the master of all non-Buddhists, expounding various phrases, flavors, causes, conditions, and parables as adornments."
I replied again: "Brahmin! There is that which belongs to no one;
it is not a non-doctrine, nor is it a matter of various phrases and expressions being neither spoken nor unspoken, nor is it without the adornment of causes and similes."
The brāhmaṇa asked:
"What is it that is not worldly discourse, not a non-doctrine, and not a non-exposition? I then replied:

“O Brahmin! There is a discourse that is not of the world, which you followers of external paths cannot know, because you are attached to false and deceptive conceptualizations regarding the unreal nature of external objects. This refers to the non-arising of conceptualization through the realization that existence and non-existence are merely the manifestations of one’s own mind; it is the non-arising of conceptualization, the non-acceptance of external sensory objects, and the eternal cessation of conceptualization—this is called the discourse that is not of the world.”
"This is my Dharma; it does not belong to you, O Brahmin!

Briefly stated, that consciousness—whether coming or going, dying or being born, pleasure or pain, sinking or seeing, touching or clinging to various signs, whether in combination or continuity, or as craving, or as attachment through causal reckoning—is [not yours]."
"O Brahmin! Such as these are your worldly doctrines; they do not belong to me.
Thus spoke Mahāmati.

When the world-renowned Brahmin asked such questions, I answered him thus; he then remained silent and withdrew without further objection, reflecting upon his own sphere of understanding and thinking to himself:

"The Śramaṇa son of the Śākyas has emerged beyond the reach of ordinary logic, teaching non-arising, signlessness, and causelessness, whereby one awakens to the fact that these are merely manifestations of one's own deluded thoughts, and that such deluded perceptions do not truly arise."
This is the Tathāgata’s account, for the sake of Mahāmati, of the questions posed by the Brahmin and the Buddha’s responses thereto.

However, as for those questions—which took two or three of the Buddha’s own doctrines as their starting points—the Buddha answered them all with worldly discourse (loka-vāda); this was done in accordance with what [the questioner] already knew.

Whenever the mental consciousness flows, following after sensory objects and becoming attached to them, it makes no distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox; all such instances constitute worldly discourse. It is for this reason that one prevents them from finding words to express themselves, thereby blocking such tendencies.
When that treatise was exhausted, there followed a request for a discourse that was not of the Lokāyata school.
The Tathāgata said, "There is that which is not yours. This was not because he did not hold it as his own tenet;

rather, even when he spoke of non-existence regarding everything down to the ornaments of similes, he did so to distinguish his teaching from theirs. Although he opened the way slightly, he ultimately did not yet speak of the ultimate reality.
When he requested it again, saying, "What is meant by 'neither a non-position nor a non-exposition'?
the Master once more suppressed him, saying, "This is not within your knowledge.

Because he was conceptually attached to external dharmas through false imagination, not only was he unable to enter into faith, but there was also fear that he would produce interpretations based on mere words, thereby increasing his views and delusions; for this reason, the Master posed this difficult challenge.
Thereafter, he says: "It is called the non-arising of false conceptualization.

He causes [the student] to realize that existence and non-existence are nothing other than what is manifested by the mind alone; thus, false conceptualization does not arise. When one no longer receives external objects, false conceptualization ceases forever. This is what is meant by "not being a worldly doctrine."

Only now do I realize that the Buddhas of the three periods of time have never bestowed a single dharma upon others; they merely cause deluded thoughts not to arise, and then the wondrous nature of true heaven will be restored without being far sought.

Having thus set forth the correct doctrine, he further refutes their errors; from the brief explanation of whether that consciousness comes or goes, up to its attachment to causes, all are the deluded consciousnesses of those externalists' calculations.
Once that treatise was refuted, he withdrew in shame, having no leisure even to offer a formal rebuttal; he merely remarked, "I shall consider it from the standpoint of my own understanding.

He further stated, "That which transcends one's own understanding"—these were all words spoken by the non-Buddhist upon his retreat and subsequent reflection. Having sought [the truth] within himself according to what the Buddha had taught and failed to find it, he first realized it lay beyond his own comprehension, and thus spoke of "non-arising," "signlessness," and so forth.
Observing what they have mastered, it is sufficient to see that they have indeed attained something. "Mahāmati!
This is precisely what you asked me earlier: why I said that those who frequent worldly treatises and engage in various forms of sophistry embrace greed and do not embrace the Dharma."
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "What is called 'craving' refers to grasping or rejecting, touching or savoring; being fettered by attachment to external objects and falling into the views of the two extremes, one further gives rise to the aggregates of suffering—birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress. This concludes the questions and answers regarding the joining of the fingers.
Mahāmati then further inquired about the meaning of desire (*rāga*) and the Dharma; in the reply, desire was defined as grasping and rejecting.
Greed is itself an affliction; because of greed, one becomes bound to and attached to external objects and the like, which constitutes the karma of fetters.

Furthermore, craving arises from associating with worldly treatises and those who propound such treatises—namely, people—who are all capable of inducing greed through their influence; therefore, it is said that they "govern and receive greed."
To say that one does not "appropriately grasp the Dharma" means that one does not appropriately grasp the True Dharma.
"Mahāmati, what is the appropriate grasping of the Dharma?"

This refers to the skillful realization that all is but the manifestation of one’s own mind; seeing the marks of both the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena, so that false conceptualization no longer arises; skillfully knowing the ever-higher stages (*uttarottara-bhūmi*); being free from mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and mentation (*manovijñāna*); receiving the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) of the wisdom of all Buddhas; fully embracing the ten inexhaustible phrases; and attaining sovereign mastery over all phenomena without effort. This is called the Dharma—namely, not falling into any views, any deceptions, any false conceptualizations, any intrinsic natures, or any dualistic extremes.
Mahāmati! Many foolish outsiders fall into the two extremes of either eternalism or nihilism.
Those who are not wise, by accepting the doctrine of causelessness, give rise to the view of eternalism.
When external causes perish and causal conditions lack intrinsic nature, one gives rise to the view of annihilationism.
Mahāmati! Because I do not perceive arising, abiding, or ceasing, I designate them as "dharmas."

Regarding the phrase "skillfully awakening to and knowing," etc.: this refers to that which is subsumed by the statement that there are no separate dharmas apart from what is grasped; rather, it means awakening to the fact that all is a manifestation of mind-only, seeing the two kinds of selflessness, not grasping at signs, being free from all conceptualization, skillfully knowing the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*), transcending mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), receiving the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) of all Buddhas, fully undertaking and practicing the ten great vows, and attaining mastery over all phenomena—this is called the benefit of the Dharma.
Furthermore, the statement "not falling into any views" and so forth means to reveal that its intrinsic nature is free from all perversions and errors.

The passage beginning with "Many non-Buddhists and ordinary people" indicates that those who fall into extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are all the dharma of fools and not of the wise; namely, the false views of annihilationism and eternalism, which are not the wisdom of the Lesser Vehicle.

The theory of causelessness (ahetuvāda) means that the nature of the four great elements is eternal and does not depend on causes for its formation; thus, one falls into the view of eternalism (śāśvatadṛṣṭi).
Alternatively, seeing external causes perish and being led to reckon that causes and conditions lack intrinsic nature, one then falls into the view of nihilism (ucchedadṛṣṭi).

Furthermore, as for the statement, "I do not perceive arising, abiding, or ceasing," it means that there is arising yet no arising, abiding yet no abiding, and ceasing yet no ceasing; this is distinct from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, and is therefore called the Dharma.

The first four lines of the verse describe the calculations of worldly discourse regarding the created and the uncreated; not knowing that [all is] merely the measure of one's own mind, they take existence and non-existence as their tenets.

Regarding the phrase "the agent and the object of action": "agent" refers to the creator, while "object of action" refers to the phenomena produced, such as the imagined arising of Brahmā, atoms, and so forth.

As for "only I," the Buddha meant that he alone takes his own mind as the primary tenet; having departed from the false imagination of agent and object, he taught this True Dharma to his disciples so that they would not study worldly doctrines.

That the measure of the mind is invisible means that because the mind is free from attachment to intrinsic nature, it cannot be seen in terms of existence or non-existence, nor can it be subsumed under the categories of subject and object; this is called being free from both the views of annihilationism and eternalism.
The two minds are precisely the views of existence and non-existence.

When the mind is driven by the notions of annihilationism and eternalism, it constitutes worldly discourse; when the mind is free from conceptual discrimination and is not so driven, this is the clear vision of one's own mind.

If those non-Buddhists reckon that "coming" constitutes birth and "going" constitutes extinction, then this matter is precisely the matter of birth and death; that which does not manifest is extinction.

Śākyamuni teaches that there is neither going nor coming, which is precisely neither birth nor extinction; therefore it is said: "Clearly understanding going and coming, delusive thoughts no longer arise."
The final four lines merely recite worldly discourse, as can be seen from the text itself.
