The Buddha told Mahāmati:

“There are some non-Buddhists who, through the cessation of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas), become detached from sense objects and perceive the impermanence of phenomena. They hold that the categories of mind and mental factors do not arise; they do not dwell upon past, future, or present objects; and as all sensations and aggregates are exhausted—like the extinguishing of a lamp or the destruction of a seed—their false imaginings no longer arise. Such individuals conceive of this state as Nirvana.”
"Mahāmati! It is not by the destruction of views that one calls it nirvāṇa.
This clearly distinguishes the nirvāṇa attained by the two vehicles, as discussed previously, from the nirvāṇa of the non-Buddhists, who take the cessation of deluded consciousness to be nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there is another request I have: fearing that the principles may not yet be fully elucidated or that misconceptions may not yet be entirely refuted, one might fall into false views. If this occurs, the path to ultimate liberation and the city of unsurpassed *nirvāṇa* would be undermined, and the originally existent *dharmakāya* and the life-force of wisdom could not be manifested.
This is a great concern for Mahāmati; it must not be that he does not inquire further. The Tathāgata then said:

"There are some non-Buddhists who conceive the notion of *nirvāṇa* regarding the extinction of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*). According to the commentary on Deva’s treatise, there are twenty types of such false conceptualizations of *nirvāṇa* held by non-Buddhists; this is the first. The treatise states:
"The exhaustion of all the aggregates of sensation—like the extinguishing of a lamp, the destruction of a seed, or the ceasing of the wind—is called *nirvāṇa*."
The present text further states: "Detachment from sense objects (*viṣaya-vairāgya*) and so forth" means being unstained by the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*); hence it is called detachment.

Because one perceives all phenomena (*dharma*) as impermanent (*anitya*), the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) do not arise. Since one does not dwell upon past or present objects, the aggregates of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) are exhausted, like the extinguishing of a lamp or the destruction of a seed.
When sensation ceases, perception ceases; hence it is said that "deluded perceptions do not arise," which is stated specifically in reference to the cessation of perception.
In reality, however, the view of perception has not been eliminated; therefore, he refutes this by stating, "It is not by destroying views that one attains nirvana."
This is a general refutation of all such views. "Mahāmati,
some maintain that liberation consists in moving from one direction to another, wherein the perception of objective realms ceases just as the wind subsides."
Alternatively, some perceive the destruction of the grasper and the grasped as liberation.
Others conceive the notions of permanence and impermanence as liberation.

Still others perceive various marks and conceptualizations as the causes that bring about the arising of suffering; having reflected upon this, they fail to discern through right awareness that these are merely manifestations of their own minds. Fearing these marks, they perceive the markless and develop a deep attachment to it, conceiving it to be *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding "from direction to direction," the *Śāstra* states:

"The second class of non-Buddhists asserts that there is an original direction (*diś*), from which the world and human beings are produced; humans are born within heaven and earth, and through successive cycles of extinction and emergence, they return to that very place."
To say that direction is permanent is called the cause of nirvāṇa.

Alternatively, it may be said that "direction" (fang) refers to a location (fang-so), which also implies "this and that"; that is, from that [place] to this [place], one does not lose one's original nature.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the cessation of the perception of objects is like the subsiding of the wind," a new commentary says:
"The Vāyu-ṛṣi heretics reckon that the wind can produce and destroy all things; they claim the nature of the wind is eternal, and this they call Nirvana."
Some may say that when the wind ceases, there is simply no trace left.
Regarding the statement "the perceiver and the perceived," etc., the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) speak of "awakening" (jñāna), which they mostly refer to as conceptualization (saṃjñā).
As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Not perceiving the perceiver and the perceived is called nirvāṇa."
"To see destruction is itself non-seeing.
Regarding the terms "permanent" and "impermanent," according to the treatise, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) say:

"The teacher is named Īśvara; his form is invisible, he pervades all places, and he is able to produce the myriad things. That which produces is permanent and is called *nirvāṇa*; the things produced are called impermanent."
Liberation and nirvāṇa are names for what is identical in essence despite differing in designation.

As for the mention of "various marks and perceptions" (*nimitta-saṃjñā*) and so forth, these take marks and perceptions as the cause of suffering; failing to realize that marks are manifestations of one's own mind, one abandons marks and clings to the view of the markless (*animitta*), taking delight in this and regarding it as nirvāṇa.

"Or there are those who perceive that the specific and general characteristics of all internal and external phenomena exist as an indestructible nature in the past, future, and present, and thus conceive the notion of nirvana."
Some say that the destruction of all dharmas—the self, the person, sentient beings, and the life-span—is the conception of nirvāṇa.

Others, whose wisdom has been scorched by the evil of non-Buddhist paths, perceive a primal nature (*prakṛti*) and a person (*puruṣa*); they hold that there is an interval between these two, and that which is produced by the person is called the primal nature. Like the analogy of primordial darkness (*tamas*), they maintain that the *guṇas* undergo transformation; the *guṇas* are the creator, and they conceive this to be nirvāṇa.

Some claim it is the exhaustion of merit and demerit; some claim it is the exhaustion of all afflictions; some claim it is wisdom; or they perceive Īśvara as the true creator of birth and death, conceiving of him as Nirvāṇa.

Regarding the statement "to awaken to and know all phenomena, both internal and external," this refers to awakening to the phenomena of the sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and so forth, as well as their specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and the distinctions of the three periods of time; it is the realization that the nature of the self (*ātman*) is indestructible and constitutes *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the phrase "self, person, and so forth," it refers to the false claim that the extinction and destruction of the four marks of existence constitutes *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the phrase "evil burns wisdom," this means that the fire of wrong views incinerates and destroys right knowledge.
Self-nature (*svabhāva*) is the root of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
The person (*pudgala*) is one of the sixteen types of views.
There is an interval between those two; "interval" means difference—that is, there is an interval and a difference between that self-nature and the person.
However, the primal nature (*prakṛti*) arises from the Spirit (*puruṣa*), analogous to the way intellect (*buddhi*) arises from primordial darkness (*tamas*).

Alternatively, some claim there are two existences: one existence arising from the primordial [nature] as intellect, and another existence arising from the objects (*viṣaya*) as the Great One (*mahat*). Such an interpretation lacks coherence with the textual meaning; if one follows that view, it would be inconsistent.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that it is like the primordial darkness (*ādyatamas*), and that the *guṇas* undergo transformation (*pariṇāma*) and so forth: this means that based on the transformation of self-nature (*svabhāva*), one regards the capacity to produce all phenomena as *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the mention of "merit" and "non-merit," non-merit refers to transgression; it means that when both transgression and merit are exhausted, this state of total exhaustion is designated as *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the phrase "the exhaustion of afflictions" (*kleśakṣaya*) and so forth, according to the treatise, afflictions and wisdom are fundamentally considered one and the same; thus, the exhaustion of afflictions based upon wisdom is called *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the phrase "or seeing Īśvara and so forth," the treatise states:
"If one holds that Īśvara can create the birth and death of all kings, then that which is capable of such creation is called 'eternal,' and is taken to be *nirvāṇa*."

"Or some say that birth and death arise through a continuous succession of mutual production, and that there is no other cause for them; such a view is an attachment to causality. Yet those fools are unable to perceive this, and because they do not know it, they conceive the notion of nirvana."
Some non-Buddhists claim to have attained the path of ultimate truth and conceive of it as nirvana.
Others, perceiving various merits, conceive of nirvana in terms of the arising of merit, its conjunction with or separation from it, or both together and not together.

Or they see the nature arising as the variegated patterns of a peacock’s plumage and various kinds of jewels, as well as the nature of sharp thorns; having seen these, they conceive the notion that this is *nirvāṇa*.

As for what is called "arising through mutual succession," the teacher of the Nirgrantha school calculates that at the beginning of the eon one male and one female were born, who then united and gave rise to beings through mutual succession. When all things perish, they return to that [source], maintaining that there is no other cause beyond this. They do not realize that such attachment is itself the cause of birth and death; yet, out of ignorance and lack of awakening, they take it to be *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the phrase "attaining the path of true reality" and so forth: the Sāṃkhya masters postulate twenty-five principles (*tattva*). They hold that from the primordial darkness (*avyakta*), [the principles] arise; they consider the realization of the path of true reality to be *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding "or seeing merit and so forth": generally, what non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) refer to as "merit" mostly points to ascetic practices; they nevertheless form fourfold conceptual views regarding the locus where these arise and their conjunction, taking this to be nirvana.
Regarding the phrase "or seeing self-nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth," the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:

"Some reckon that all things arise spontaneously; the variegated patterns of a peacock's feathers, the sharpness of thorns, and the various jewels produced from places where gems are found—by whom could such things have been made?"
They then grasp at spontaneity (*svabhāva*) as being *nirvāṇa*.
"Mahāmati! There are some who perceive the twenty-five principles (*tattva*)."
Some, having been protected by kings and having studied the *Ṣaḍdharmaprakaraṇa*, conceive the notion that this is nirvāṇa.
Others, seeing that time is the creator—that the world is governed by the seasons—conceive such an awakening to be nirvāṇa.

Some say it is existence-nature, some say it is non-existence-nature; some say they know existence-nature and non-existence-nature; or, perceiving a distinction between awakening and nirvana, they form the conception of nirvana.
"Awakening to the twenty-five realities" means awakening to the reality of the twenty-five principles (*tattva*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the king protects the nation," it means that if one can receive and practice the *Ṣāḍguṇya-śāstra*, the myriad people will be brought to peace and happiness; this nature of peace and happiness is taken as *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the statement that "time is the agent": the teachers of the *Kālavāda* (Time-Theory) maintain that time is the cause capable of producing all phenomena of the world; although time undergoes transformation, the agent remains unchanged, and those who perceive it thus consider this to be *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the statement "the nature is neither existent nor non-existent," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"Some cling to the existence of things, some cling to the non-existence of things, and some cling to both the existence and non-existence of things, taking these to be nirvāṇa."
This refers to "nature" (*prakṛti*); nature is the dharma, and the dharma is the thing itself.

As for the statement that there is "awakening" and so forth, it means that while the myriad things are clamorous and active, nirvāṇa is quiescent; yet these two are without distinction, and this constitutes nirvāṇa.
The above are the various false conceptualizations of non-Buddhists that give rise to views of nirvāṇa; their characteristics are explained in detail, as in the treatises of Āryadeva and others.
"There are such various delusions as these, spoken by non-Buddhists, which fail to establish what they seek to establish and are rejected by the wise."
Mahāmati! All such [views] fall into the two extremes and are conceived as nirvāṇa.
Such false imaginings of nirvāṇa held by these outsiders are entirely devoid of either arising or ceasing.

Mahāmati! Regarding each of those various non-Buddhist nirvāṇas, when examined with wisdom according to their own treatises, nothing at all is established. Just as their deluded thoughts, minds, and consciousnesses come and go, drifting and surging, there is not a single one among them who attains nirvāṇa.
This section, which concludes the refutation, consists of five points.

First, regarding the claim that "the proven is not established": because these are all merely false imaginings, even if one calculates [them] as *nirvāṇa*, they do not constitute actual *nirvāṇa*; thus, they are discarded by the wise. This is the first point.
Furthermore, it says: "That 'all such things fall into the two extremes' refers to the second [point].
Moreover, although they falsely conceptualize arising and ceasing, in reality, how could those dharmas ever arise or cease? This is the third [point]."
However, all those calculations are heterodox doctrines; when examined with correct wisdom, they are found to be unestablished—this is the fourth point.
Furthermore, because their mental conceptions are in flux and contrary to the nature of nirvāṇa, there is consequently no one who attains nirvāṇa—this is the fifth point.
By this analysis, it is sufficient to reveal its falsity. "Mahāmati!

That which I call nirvāṇa refers to the excellent realization of the manifestation of one's own mind, non-attachment to external natures, and being free from the four extremes (*catuskoṭi*). It is seeing the state of reality as it is, not falling into the two extremes of the false imaginings of one's own mental manifestations, and the non-apprehension of the grasped and the grasper. Since no conclusion is reached by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the foolish should not cling to what is unreal; having abandoned that, one attains the noble dharma of self-realization. Knowing the two kinds of selflessness, being free from the two afflictions, purifying the two obstacles, and forever departing from the two deaths, one reaches the successive stages up to the stage of the Tathāgata. Being free from mind, thought, and mentation, and possessing various profound samādhis such as those like shadows and illusions, it is called nirvāṇa."
“Mahāmati! You and the other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice and study this; you must swiftly distance yourselves from all views of nirvāṇa held by the various non-Buddhists.
The phrase “as I have taught” and so forth refers to revealing the correct [teaching] in contrast to the erroneous.
Its contents are also fivefold:
first, to skillfully realize that which is the manifestation of one's own mind and not to cling to external natures;
second, to transcend the four extremes and perceive the state of reality as it is.
Third, by not falling into the two extremes of false conceptualization regarding the manifestations of one's own mind, the grasper and the grasped are found to be unobtainable.
Fourth, the fact that no object of establishment is seen through any measurement reveals that the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa transcends all heterodox and external views.

"Measurement" refers to number. Regarding "the foolish should not grasp at what is real": "foolish" means deluded; that is, being deluded regarding the true principle, one should not cling to whatever is perceived—this is the fifth.

Regarding the phrase "having abandoned that," it means that once one has abandoned those false views, one immediately attains the dharma of self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*). One realizes the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*), becomes free from both the pervasive and specific delusions, eliminates the two obstacles of afflictions and knowledge (*kleśa-jñeyāvaraṇa*), and leaves behind both birth-and-death through分段 (*bhavasaṃsāra*) and birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāmika-saṃsāra*). Thus, by gradually traversing the various stages (*bhūmi*) until reaching the stage of Buddhahood—these are all the dharmas that are realized.

The *māyopama-samādhi* (illusion-like samādhi) transcends mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*); it is precisely because of this that it can manifest *nirvāṇa*. To investigate the *nirvāṇa* of the three virtues—that which is called the Tathāgata’s secret treasury—it is like the three dots of the letter *i* or the three eyes of the Lord of Devas: neither vertical nor horizontal, beyond thought and beyond discourse. Abiding thus is the ultimate *nirvāṇa*; therefore, I admonish students that they should practice and study this, and abandon those false views.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The views of nirvana held by the heterodox teachers Each give rise to false imaginings;
These arise from mental conceptions And lack the skillful means for liberation."
The fool, bound by fetters, remains far removed from skillful means;
with the notion of liberation held by outsiders, liberation will never arise.
The various wisdoms of the many paths are all encompassed within the vision of the outsiders.
"They all lack liberation, because of their foolishness and deluded conceptualization.
This verse refers to the various views of non-Buddhists regarding their false calculations of *nirvāṇa*.
The term "each" refers to the twenty-one different types listed in the preceding text; however, they all arise from the mental conceptions of perverse habitual tendencies.

Regarding the statement that there is no skillful means for liberation: if one wishes to untie the bonds of birth and death to attain liberation, it cannot be achieved without the practice of skillful means.
Since there is neither skillful means nor liberation, how can one enter nirvana?

To be "foolish" is to be deluded; because of this delusion, one fails to realize that the false views one clings to are the very bonds of affliction and birth-and-death. Thus, by abandoning skillful means while desiring liberation, one will ultimately never attain it.
The four lines beginning with "The various knowledges" state that the supernatural powers and wisdom attained through the ascetic practices of non-Buddhists are false and not real.
"All deluded non-Buddhists, Through false views, posit agent and action, And debate the categories of existence and non-existence; None of them possess liberation."
Ordinary fools delight in false conceptualization, And do not hear the wisdom of reality.
Verbal expression is the root of the three sufferings; Reality is the cause for extinguishing suffering.
It is like an image in a mirror: Though it appears, it does not exist.
In the mirror-like mind of delusive thought, the ignorant perceive duality.
Failing to recognize the mind and its objects, they give rise to dualistic delusions;
by thoroughly understanding the mind and its spheres, such delusions do not arise.
"The mind itself is manifold; it is far removed from the characteristic and the characterized.
Though phenomena appear, they do not truly appear—just like the deluded imaginings of the ignorant.
The phrase "all foolish non-Buddhists falsely perceive the agent and the acted" concludes by refuting externalist calculations.

The passage "Existence and non-existence are below" clarifies the reality of false imagination (*vikalpa*). This means that false imagination arises from verbal discourse and serves as the root of the three types of suffering; reality, being the opposite of false imagination, is therefore the cause for extinguishing suffering. The intent is simply to lead the ignorant and foolish to turn back from delusion and return to awakening.

To further clarify this through analogy: the mirror represents the mind, and the image represents the reflection. Because ordinary beings cannot comprehend that objects are merely mind, they perceive phenomena as existing outside the mind and give rise to conceptual discrimination. This is like seeing an image in a mirror and conceiving of it as real; thus, they perceive duality. Therefore, it is said: "Failing to recognize the mind and its conditions, one gives rise to dualistic delusions."
"Object" (*ālambana*) refers to the external realm; if one realizes that mind and object are of one suchness, from where could delusion arise?
The four lines following the word "mind" correspond to the preceding metaphor of the mirror and its images, representing the various kinds of objective realms.
Once one knows that all objects are merely mind, there is neither the perceiving subject nor the perceived object.

"Phenomena" refers to the objective realm; the manifestation of these phenomena and their objects is like reflections in a mirror, lacking any reality. It is only because of delusion and ignorance that one fails to understand this and gives rise to conceptual discrimination within oneself.
"The three realms of existence are mere conceptual construction; external objects do not exist at all.
Conceptual construction manifests in various ways, yet the ignorant and foolish cannot comprehend this.
Throughout the sūtras it is taught that conceptual construction never transcends names."
"If one is apart from verbal expression, there is likewise nothing to be expressed.

The "three existences" (trabhava) refers to the three realms; "external objects" (bāhyārtha) refers to external environments. This means that the cycle of birth and death within the three realms and six paths has no substantial reality; it is merely through deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that these various external objects are perceived. Therefore, it is said: "The ignorant and foolish cannot comprehend this."
This is a summary of the faults of delusion.

However, the various dharmas taught by the Tathāgata all describe how sentient beings are immersed in birth and death due to their false imaginings; his intention is to cause sentient beings to turn away from delusion and return to the truth, so that they may dwell securely in nirvāṇa.
Yet sentient beings cling to names and verbal expressions, unable to forget the words to grasp the meaning;

if one can thoroughly understand that verbal expression is itself non-expression, then even the Dharma being taught cannot be apprehended—just as when one has obtained the fish or the rabbit, one forgets the trap or the snare. This is the profound intention with which the Tathāgata reveals himself to people.
Commentary on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Fascicle Three, Part Two.
